brief description: Soviet probe aimed at the Moon. First man-made object to touch another celestial body, deliberately crashed near Autolycus.
American probe meant to photograph the Moon and drop a seismic capsule. An onboard computer failure made it hit the far side without transmitting any data.
American probe intended to photograph the surface until impact. Impact occurred as planned, but the cameras failed and returned no images.
First success of the Ranger program: more than 4,000 close-up images transmitted before impact, to prepare the Apollo landings.
Photography of candidate sites for Apollo: more than 7,000 images transmitted before the deliberate impact.
Last Ranger probe: images relayed live on television during the fall toward the Alphonsus crater.
First Soviet attempt at a soft landing. Braking failed and the probe crashed.
Another soft-landing attempt: an orientation problem prevented proper braking and the probe crashed.
Another soft-landing attempt: the retrorockets fired too late and the probe crashed.
First soft landing in history. Transmitted the first panoramic photos taken from the lunar surface.
First American probe to land softly: test of the landing technique and more than 11,000 photos to prepare Apollo.
American lander intended to test soft landing. A correction engine did not work, the probe began spinning on itself and crashed.
American orbiter that mapped landing sites for Apollo and took the first photo of Earth seen from the Moon. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Soviet lander that studied the lunar soil (strength, density, radiation) and transmitted panoramas.
American lander equipped with a scoop to analyze the soil. Visited by the Apollo 12 crew in 1969.
American lander to study the soil. Contact was lost a few minutes before landing, probably after an engine failure.
First on-site chemical analysis of the lunar soil, after a hard landing.
American orbiter that photographed landing sites for Apollo. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
American orbiter that photographed landing sites for Apollo. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Soil analysis and first liftoff from the Moon (a small hop of a few meters) to test the engines.
Last Surveyor: study of rugged highland terrain near the Tycho crater.
Last orbiter of the series: mapping of nearly the entire Moon. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
First crewed landing. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon and brought back about 21 kg of samples.
Soviet sample-return probe, launched in competition with Apollo 11. It crashed during descent.
Precision landing near Surveyor 3. Installation of scientific instruments and retrieval of parts of Surveyor 3.
Ascent stage of the lunar module, deliberately launched against the Moon to be recorded by the seismometer left on site.
Upper stage of the Saturn V rocket directed toward the Moon so that the Apollo 12 seismometer would record the impact. Apollo 13 itself did not land on the Moon.
First automatic return of lunar samples: about 100 g of soil brought back to Earth.
Deployed Lunokhod 1, the first remote-controlled rover on another celestial body, which traveled about 10 km.
Upper stage of the Saturn V rocket directed toward the Moon for seismic measurements.
Mission to Fra Mauro, the intended destination of Apollo 13: samples, scientific instruments and seismology experiments.
Ascent stage of the lunar module, deliberately launched against the Moon for seismic measurements.
Upper stage of the Saturn V rocket directed toward the Moon for seismic measurements.
First mission with a lunar rover: exploration of Hadley–Apennine and more than 75 kg of samples.
Ascent stage of the lunar module, deliberately launched against the Moon for seismic measurements.
Soviet sample-return probe to the highlands. It probably crashed during descent.
Sample return from the highlands: about 55 g of soil brought back to Earth.
First exploration of the lunar highlands, on the Descartes plateau, with a lunar rover and about 95 kg of samples.
Upper stage of the Saturn V rocket directed toward the Moon for seismic measurements.
Last crewed mission on the Moon to date: exploration of Taurus–Littrow with geologist Harrison Schmitt, about 110 kg of samples.
Ascent stage of the lunar module, deliberately launched against the Moon for seismic measurements.
Deployed Lunokhod 2, a rover that traveled about 39 km in the Le Monnier crater.
Sample-return probe in Mare Crisium. Damaged on landing, it could not drill the soil and no samples came back.
Last Soviet sample return: about 170 g of soil collected down to a depth of 2 m.
First Japanese probe to the Moon, which tested fuel-efficient trajectories. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Orbiter that mapped the Moon's composition and gravity and detected hydrogen at the poles. Crashed into a polar crater to search for water.
European probe that tested ion propulsion and mapped the Moon. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Impact probe released by the Indian orbiter Chandrayaan-1 to analyze the lunar atmosphere during its fall. It detected water.
Small relay satellite of the Kaguya mission, used to measure the gravity of the far side. Crashed at the end of the mission.
First Chinese orbiter: 3D mapping of the Moon. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Japanese orbiter that mapped the Moon's topography, gravity and composition in detail. Crashed at the end of the mission.
Rocket stage deliberately crashed into a polar crater to raise a plume and search for water.
Companion probe that flew through the plume of the Centaur stage before crashing in turn. Presence of water confirmed.
One of the two twin probes that measured the lunar gravity field to study the Moon's interior. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
Second GRAIL twin probe, deliberately crashed 30 seconds after Ebb.
First soft landing since 1976: lander and Yutu rover to study lunar geology and environment.
American orbiter that studied the Moon's very tenuous atmosphere and its dust. Deliberately crashed at the end of the mission.
First landing on the far side, with the Yutu-2 rover, thanks to the Queqiao relay satellite.
First landing attempt by a private mission (SpaceIL). Main engine failure and crash during descent.
Vikram lander and Pragyan rover aimed at the south pole region. Contact lost at an altitude of about 2 km.
Sample-return mission: about 1.7 kg of soil collected then brought back to Earth.
Ascent stage deliberately discarded onto the Moon after the sample transfer.
Upper stage of a Chinese rocket abandoned in orbit, which accidentally fell on the far side, creating a double crater.
First landing attempt by the Japanese company ispace. An altitude estimation error caused the crash.
First Russian mission to the Moon since 1976, aimed at the south pole. A failed orbit maneuver caused the crash.
First successful landing near the lunar south pole, with the Pragyan rover, to study the soil and search for water.
Precision landing demonstration. Landed within 100 m of the target, but on its back.
First American commercial landing (Intuitive Machines), with NASA payloads. Landed but tipped over.
First sample return from the far side: about 2 kg of soil collected.
Ascent stage discarded onto the Moon after the sample transfer.
Commercial mission by Firefly for NASA: 10 scientific payloads, fully successful mission.
Second Intuitive Machines mission, to prospect for ice near the south pole. Tipped over on landing, mission greatly shortened.
Second ispace landing attempt, with a small rover. Contact lost before landing, crash.
SpaceX rocket stage, launched in January 2025 with Blue Ghost and Hakuto-R, which fell accidentally. Crater of about 18 m photographed by Danuri then LRO.
